name: Pioglitazone

lead: Pioglitazone is a generic prescription pill for type 2 diabetes. It comes up in appearance discussion because it is known to raise subcutaneous fat, which people connect to changing where body fat sits.

It activates PPAR-gamma receptors, mainly in fat tissue, muscle and liver, which lowers insulin resistance, and weight gain from added subcutaneous fat is a recognised effect. No human study has tested it for cosmetic purposes.

paras: Its documented use is as a daily diabetes pill under prescription. In one forum context it has also been discussed as a topical under-eye product.
The label has a boxed warning for congestive heart failure and lists edema and fractures. Bladder cancer warnings were added in 2011. It is prescription only, and no cosmetic use is approved.

social.title: Pioglitazone: An anti-diabetic compound with anti-aging properties

angle.text: Pioglitazone is known to raise subcutaneous fat storage, so appearance discussions bring it up in connection with changing body-fat distribution. It is studied for type 2 diabetes, and no human study has tested cosmetic use.

lead: Pioglitazone (brand name Actos) is an oral type 2 diabetes drug in the thiazolidinedione class. It was developed by Takeda, patented in 1985, came into medical use in 1999 and is now generic.[1][2] It is prescribed to lower blood glucose by reducing insulin resistance.

It activates the PPAR-gamma receptor, which is found in fat, muscle and liver tissue, and reduces insulin resistance.[3][1] PPAR-gamma is a central regulator of fat cell development, and a known effect of the drug is mild weight gain attributed to increased subcutaneous fat; this is the link that appearance-focused discussion draws on.[3][1] Its label carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure.[3]

Pioglitazone appears in appearance-related discussion mainly because of this action on fat tissue. Thiazolidinediones as a class increase fatty-acid storage and promote the formation of fat cells in subcutaneous fat, which is why some people with an interest in facial or body fat distribution discuss them, and why a small number of forum users have proposed home-made topical under-eye preparations.[4] No published human study has tested pioglitazone for cosmetic purposes, and no cosmetic use is approved.

paras: The US label indicates pioglitazone as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, alone or with other agents; it is not for type 1 diabetes or ketoacidosis.[3] Early reviews of trials involving over 4,500 patients reported falls in HbA1c and favourable lipid changes when used alone or with sulphonylureas, metformin and insulin.[5]

Wikipedia notes that a Cochrane review found it reduced the risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes versus placebo in people at risk, although evidence was mostly of low certainty.[1] Research uses have included non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, where randomized trials reported effects on liver histology.[6][7][8]

No approved cosmetic use exists. Online appearance communities have discussed pioglitazone in two ways: as a drug whose fat-gaining effect is relevant to people who want fuller features, and as an ingredient in home-made topical preparations for under-eye hollows or bags. A Hacker News post titled as describing pioglitazone as an anti-diabetic compound with anti-aging properties circulated in 2021.[9] No clinical studies have tested pioglitazone, topical or oral, for under-eye appearance or facial fat.

Pioglitazone is an agonist of PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor found in adipose tissue, skeletal muscle and liver; activation changes the expression of genes that regulate glucose and lipid metabolism and reduces insulin resistance without increasing insulin secretion.[3][10] It also binds the mitochondrial protein mitoNEET.[1] PPAR-gamma has been studied in adipose tissue biology, including a 2012 Nature study showing it drives the accumulation and phenotype of regulatory T cells in fat.[11]
Pioglitazone is more than 99% protein-bound and is metabolised in the liver mainly by CYP2C8, with a half-life of roughly 3 to 7 hours.[1]

sections.h: The thiazolidinedione class and fat tissue
paras: Thiazolidinediones, also called glitazones, were introduced in the late 1990s for type 2 diabetes. Troglitazone was withdrawn because of drug-induced liver injury, and as of 2024 pioglitazone and rosiglitazone are the two FDA-approved members, with lobeglitazone approved in South Korea.[4]

The central action of the class is on fat cells. By activating PPAR-gamma, which pairs with the RXR receptor to change gene transcription, these drugs increase the storage of fatty acids in adipocytes, lower circulating free fatty acids, and shift cells toward glucose oxidation.[4] They induce adipogenesis, the formation of new fat cells, in subcutaneous fat; this property has been used in some forms of lipodystrophy, where thiazolidinediones have improved insulin resistance.[4] Wikipedia also notes that transgender patients have used the effect to shift fat distribution toward a gynoid pattern.[4]

This is the biological basis for the appearance-related interest: subcutaneous fat gain is a documented effect of oral treatment, and fat volume is a determinant of facial fullness. The drug's fat effects in published work are systemic and have been described in people treated for diabetes, not in cosmetic settings.[1][4] Class effects on bone are also described: thiazolidinediones reduce bone mineral density and raise fracture risk in women, possibly by shifting marrow stromal cells toward fat cells instead of bone-forming cells.[4]

The label's boxed warning states that thiazolidinediones cause or worsen congestive heart failure in some patients; edema and fractures are also listed as warnings, and the most common reactions are upper respiratory infection, headache, sinusitis, myalgia and pharyngitis.[3] Wikipedia describes mild weight gain attributed to increased subcutaneous adipose tissue and fluid retention.[1]

In June 2011 France withdrew the drug and Germany advised against new prescriptions over bladder cancer concerns, and the FDA added a label warning in August 2011; a 2017 meta-analysis reportedly found no difference in bladder cancer rates.[1] Rare cholestatic hepatitis has been reported, and an earlier drug of the class, troglitazone, was withdrawn for liver toxicity.[1][5] A 2007 meta-analysis of randomized trials found fewer ischemic cardiac events but more heart failure.[12]
Safety in pregnancy has not been established; the label says limited human data cannot determine risk, and animal studies showed no adverse developmental effects at the tested exposures.[3]

No studies found of pioglitazone for appearance or cosmetic purposes. Studies in medical conditions are extensive. The PROactive trial in 5,238 high-risk people with type 2 diabetes found no difference in its primary composite endpoint, though some secondary outcomes favoured pioglitazone.[1] Trials in steatohepatitis include a 96-week trial of 247 non-diabetic adults comparing pioglitazone, vitamin E and placebo,[6] an earlier placebo-controlled trial in people with impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes,[7] and a long-term trial in people with prediabetes or diabetes.[8] Network meta-analyses have ranked pioglitazone among treatments for liver outcomes in metabolic steatohepatitis and in people with both fatty liver and diabetes.[13][14] A trial after stroke or transient ischemic attack has also been published.[15]

Takeda patented pioglitazone in 1985 and it entered medical use in 1999.[1] The US FDA approval date is given as 15 July 1999 in one summary.[2] Sales exceeded $2.4 billion in 2008, and the first US generic was approved on 17 August 2012.[1] In 2023 it was among the most prescribed drugs in the US.[1]

Pioglitazone is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.[1] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a fat-affecting drug. The best-known thread proposes a home-made topical mixture of pioglitazone with a skin-penetration enhancer for under-eye hollows, bags and tissue support, in which the author argues that PPAR-gamma activation promotes local fat growth and reduces inflammation. Replies in that thread are brief and mostly ask for a ready-made cream instead.

Outside appearance communities, pioglitazone has attracted interest from longevity and biohacking readers; a 2021 Hacker News post framed it as an anti-diabetic compound with anti-aging properties and drew no discussion.[9] A systematic review of prospective studies in diabetes reported a 47% lower dementia risk among pioglitazone users in the diabetic population, a finding that circulates in those circles.[16] No published human study has tested pioglitazone applied to skin for under-eye or facial changes, and cardiovascular and other label warnings relate to systemic use.[3]

lore.intro: In appearance communities pioglitazone is discussed mainly in the context of the under-eye area and facial fat, typically as an experimental topical idea; it appears far less often than mainstream under-eye options.
